newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu shrugs off U.S., world criticism.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu shrugs off U.S., world criticism.

text.p: Israel's leader Benjamin Netanyahu shrugged off criticism by U.S. President Bill Clinton on Tuesday, vowing to start work within days on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

"It's two weeks from the standpoint of the bulldozers. From the standpoint of the survey work it's only a few days," the Israeli prime minister told army radio. "We are determined to go on building in Jerusalem.

Clinton sided with Israel's Palestinian peace partner Yasser Arafat at a White House meeting on Monday, saying Netanyahu's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews in the city subject to future negotiation would fuel "mistrust".
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it, a move not recognised internationally, to claim all the city as its capital.

The PLO, which is supposed to negotiate the city's fate with Israel in talks due to end in 1999, sees construction at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel, as an attempt to block its demand East Jerusalem become capital of a Palestinian state.
"There was nothing new in what he (Clinton) said," Netanyahu told the radio. "The Americans understand our policy well."
In Washington on Tuesday, Arafat said he had no other alternative but to press ahead with peace negotiations despite the damage caused by the housing decision.

Netanyahu has faced a drumbeat of criticism from the United States, Europe and the Arab world that could reach a crescendo on Tuesday at a U.N. Security Council debate aimed at halting the building project.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, in Jerusalem on Tuesday, said he discussed Middle East peace moves with Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy before heading into talks with Netanyahu.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel arrives in Israel on Wednesday.

"It could be the world doesn't agree to our sovereignty in Jerusalem. But we are united in agreeing that we are the sovereigns in Jerusalem," said a defiant Netanyahu. "I don't intend to be influenced by opposition of one kind or another."

He denied delaying work for fear of upsetting Egypt's leader Hosni Mubarak when they meet in Cairo on Wednesday. Mubarak has already said the project will loom large in their talks. Netanyahu cited legal and technical reasons for the delay.

The Israeli leader said he would convene a cabinet meeting this week to discuss carrying out the next withdrawal of Israeli troops from parts of the West Bank as agreed with the PLO in January. The redeployment is due to take place by Friday.
"I imagine we will begin carrying it out immediately after a decision will be taken," Netanyahu told Israel Radio.

In a bid to blunt criticism of the building project, Israel said it would allow another 3,000 homes for Arabs in East Jerusalem. Peace activists dismissed the announcement as a public relations ploy unlikely to be carried out.
Israeli moves in Jerusalem sparked violence in September. Sixty-one Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers died in gunbattles after Netanyahu opened a tourist tunnel entrance near Islamic shrines.
